lanes.label: Search
lanes.question: How do we find a way?

lanes.label: Probability
lanes.question: How do we reason under uncertainty?

checkpoints.label: Breadth-first search
checkpoints.story: Start with a simple promise: explore every nearby possibility before going farther.

checkpoints.label: Depth-first search
checkpoints.story: A second way to explore leads us back to nineteenth-century mazes.

checkpoints.label: A* search
checkpoints.story: Costs and estimates meet. A route can be guided by what we know about the destination.

checkpoints.label: Minimax
checkpoints.story: Search acquires an opponent. A good move must survive someone else's best reply.

checkpoints.label: Alpha–beta pruning
checkpoints.story: Some possibilities no longer matter. Bounds let us skip work while preserving the decision.

checkpoints.label: Propositional logic
checkpoints.story: The map reaches back to symbolic logic, then forward to machines that search for proofs.

checkpoints.label: First-order logic
checkpoints.story: From whole statements to objects and relations: an older foundation opens a more expressive world.

checkpoints.label: Logic programming · Prolog
checkpoints.story: Logic becomes a programming language. Explore rule-based expert systems, build a small Prolog adviser, and see how IBM Watson used Prolog to analyze language.

checkpoints.label: Probability theory
checkpoints.story: Reasoning meets uncertainty. Events, distributions, and conditional probability give us a language for incomplete information.

checkpoints.label: Bayes' theorem
checkpoints.story: Reverse the conditioning: combine a prior with the likelihood of evidence to calculate a posterior.

checkpoints.label: Bayesian networks
checkpoints.story: A graph and local probability tables describe a joint distribution. Follow a parallel path through probabilistic logic programming, statistical relational learning, Markov logic, and ProbLog.

checkpoints.label: Inference by enumeration
checkpoints.story: Observe evidence, sum over hidden possibilities, and normalize. A small network makes the arithmetic visible.

checkpoints.label: Variable elimination
checkpoints.story: Answer the same query with factors: multiply only what is needed, sum out a hidden variable, and reuse the result.

topics.title: Breadth-first search
topics.tagline: Explore the nearest possibilities first.
topics.problem: You can move between neighboring states, but you do not know which route reaches the goal with the fewest steps. Following one appealing route too far might miss a much shorter alternative nearby.
topics.idea: Breadth-first search expands a frontier one depth at a time. A first-in, first-out queue holds discovered states; a visited set prevents repeated exploration in a graph. With equal step costs, the first goal reached has a shortest path in number of edges. That guarantee does not extend to arbitrary weighted edges.
topics.significance: BFS separates a problem's state-space representation from the policy used to explore it. Change the frontier policy and a different search method emerges. Its expanding layers also make a useful bridge from the classroom graph to practical routing problems.
topics.history: The date marks Edward Moore's published maze-search work. Lee's 1961 routing paper is another documented milestone. It should not be read as a claim that Moore uniquely invented every form of breadth-first exploration.

example.label: A frontier in layers
example.code:
S → {A, B}
A → C    B → G
Visit: S | A, B | C, G
Shortest route to G: S → B → G
example.explanation: The bars separate depths. Within a layer, the order depends on how neighbors are listed.

contributors.name: Edward F. Moore
contributors.role: Published a shortest-path maze method in 1959.

contributors.name: C. Y. Lee
contributors.role: Published a related wave-based path-connection algorithm in 1961.

milestones.label: Publication
milestones.description: Moore's The Shortest Path Through a Maze.

milestones.label: Routing application
milestones.description: Lee applies layer-based path finding to connection problems.

topics.title: Depth-first search
topics.tagline: Follow a possibility. Return when it ends.
topics.problem: A maze may have more branches than you can hold in mind. You need a systematic way to explore without continually starting over, and a record of where to return when a passage fails.
topics.idea: Depth-first search follows one branch as far as it can, then backtracks to the most recent unexplored alternative. A stack or recursive calls store the active path. For graph traversal, marking visited states prevents revisiting cycles. Its frontier is often smaller than BFS's, but the first goal it finds need not be the nearest one.
topics.significance: Backtracking turns apparent failure into useful information: this branch is exhausted, so try another. In an unbounded search tree, however, one infinite branch can prevent DFS from reaching a solution elsewhere. Termination depends on the state space and repeated-state handling.
topics.history: Lucas's 1882 maze chapter describes a method credited to Charles Pierre Trémaux. The map uses this published precursor to modern DFS, not an exact birth date for today's pseudocode. Maze traversal has several early formulations.

example.label: One branch at a time
example.code:
S → A → C  (dead end)
        ↩ A ↩ S
S → B → G  (goal)
example.explanation: Backtracking restores the last choice point. Neighbor order determines which branch is tried first.

contributors.name: Charles Pierre Trémaux
contributors.role: Devised the maze-marking method described by Lucas.

contributors.name: Édouard Lucas
contributors.role: Published an account of the maze method in 1882.

milestones.label: Published precursor
milestones.description: Lucas describes Trémaux's systematic maze traversal.

topics.title: Dijkstra's shortest paths
topics.tagline: The cheapest route so far comes first.
topics.problem: Counting steps is insufficient when edges have different costs. A route with fewer edges may be much more expensive than a longer route, so BFS's depth ordering no longer solves the weighted problem.
topics.idea: Maintain each discovered vertex's best known distance from the start. Repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance, then relax its outgoing edges. With nonnegative edge weights, a settled distance cannot later be improved through an unsettled vertex. A priority queue makes that selection efficient.
topics.significance: This gives a useful comparison with uniform-cost search in AI: both prioritize accumulated path cost. Their usual stopping conditions and problem formulations differ. Introducing an estimate of the remaining cost creates a natural technical connection to A*, without requiring a claim about personal influence.
topics.history: Dijkstra's three-page 1959 note presents both a shortest-path problem and a minimum-spanning-tree problem. This node follows the shortest-path result. Publication is the timeline milestone; it does not imply the idea was conceived on that date.

example.label: Steps versus cost
example.code:
S → G       cost 9
S → A → G   cost 2 + 3 = 5
Choose S → A → G
example.explanation: With weighted edges, two inexpensive steps can beat one expensive step.

contributors.name: Edsger W. Dijkstra
contributors.role: Published the shortest-path method in 1959.

milestones.label: Publication
milestones.description: A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs.

topics.title: A* search
topics.tagline: Add what you know to what you estimate.
topics.problem: Searching only by cost already paid may spend effort in directions far from the destination. Searching only by apparent closeness may choose an expensive route. Can the two kinds of information work together?
topics.idea: A* orders its frontier by f(n) = g(n) + h(n): the best known cost to n plus an estimate of the remaining cost. An admissible heuristic never overestimates that remainder. In graph search, consistency supports closing states without reopening them; with an inconsistent admissible heuristic, improved paths may require reopening states to preserve optimality.
topics.significance: The heuristic brings problem knowledge into a general search procedure. On a finite graph with nonnegative costs, using h = 0 gives uniform-cost ordering. A more informative valid estimate can focus exploration while preserving a least-cost solution. Tie-breaking and implementation details still affect the visited states.
topics.history: Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael's 1968 paper formalized heuristic shortest-path search. The map anchors A* to that publication and credits the three authors together.

example.label: Compare two frontier states
example.code:
A: g = 4, h = 5  → f = 9
B: g = 6, h = 2  → f = 8
Expand B next.
example.explanation: The best estimated complete route need not have the smallest cost so far.

contributors.name: Peter E. Hart
contributors.role: Co-authored the formal A* search framework.

contributors.name: Nils J. Nilsson
contributors.role: Co-authored the formal A* search framework.

contributors.name: Bertram Raphael
contributors.role: Co-authored the formal A* search framework.

milestones.label: Publication
milestones.description: A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths.

topics.title: Minimax
topics.tagline: Choose a move that survives the best reply.
topics.problem: In a game, a path to a favorable outcome is not enough: an opponent chooses some of the moves. A strategy must account for what the opponent can force, rather than assuming they will cooperate.
topics.idea: For a finite, deterministic, two-player, zero-sum game tree with perfect information, back up terminal utilities. MAX selects the largest child value; MIN selects the smallest. The resulting root value describes optimal play within that tree. When search stops early, a heuristic evaluation replaces true terminal utility, so the decision depends on the quality and depth of the approximation.
topics.significance: A search tree now represents alternating control. An attractive continuation can be rejected because the other player has a stronger response. This makes minimax a useful contrast with single-agent route finding, where the agent controls every action.
topics.history: Von Neumann's 1928 minimax theorem concerns zero-sum games and mixed strategies. It is a mathematical foundation, not the invention date of the classroom game-tree algorithm. Shannon's 1950 chess paper supplies a later computational milestone.

example.label: Back up the opponent's choices
example.code:
Left replies:  3, 8 → MIN chooses 3
Right replies: 2, 9 → MIN chooses 2
MAX chooses the left move: value 3
example.explanation: A possible payoff of 9 is no help if the opponent can force 2.

contributors.name: John von Neumann
contributors.role: Proved the 1928 minimax theorem for zero-sum games.

contributors.name: Claude E. Shannon
contributors.role: Explained minimax-style evaluation in computer chess in 1950.

milestones.label: Mathematical foundation
milestones.description: Von Neumann publishes the minimax theorem.

milestones.label: Computational formulation
milestones.description: Shannon discusses game-tree search and evaluation for chess.

topics.title: Shannon's computer chess
topics.tagline: Chess becomes a problem of selective search.
topics.problem: A computer can generate legal moves, but the number of possible games grows far too quickly for exhaustive calculation. How can a machine choose a useful move before it runs out of time?
topics.idea: Shannon describes representing board positions, generating continuations, and estimating the strength of positions when a search cannot reach the end. His discussion distinguishes broad search to a limited depth from more selective exploration of promising continuations. A board evaluation compresses strategic features into a score that can guide a decision.
topics.significance: This is a meeting point between a general search procedure and knowledge of a particular domain. The same tension remains visible in the course: spend more effort exploring, improve the evaluation of a state, or avoid exploring branches that cannot matter. Those are different ways to cope with combinatorial growth.
topics.history: The 1950 article is a program design and analysis, not a claim that Shannon had already built a championship chess machine. Its explicit search and evaluation discussion makes it a useful companion to the minimax lesson.

example.label: When the tree is too large
example.code:
Legal moves → opponent replies → …
At the depth limit:
use a board evaluation, then back up values.
example.explanation: A leaf of the searched tree may be an ordinary board position, not the end of the game.

contributors.name: Claude E. Shannon
contributors.role: Published the computer-chess design and analysis.

milestones.label: Publication
milestones.description: Programming a Computer for Playing Chess appears in Philosophical Magazine.

topics.title: Alpha–beta pruning
topics.tagline: Know enough to stop looking.
topics.problem: Minimax may inspect a large number of branches that cannot change the final decision. Once another option is already better, fully evaluating a losing alternative can be wasted work.
topics.idea: Carry bounds through the game tree: alpha records a lower bound available to MAX, while beta records an upper bound available to MIN. When the bounds establish that a branch cannot improve an ancestor's choice, stop exploring it. On the same fixed tree with the same evaluations, correct alpha–beta search returns the minimax value; move ordering affects how much work is saved.
topics.significance: This is a certificate for skipping work. A branch is pruned because a bound makes its remaining details irrelevant to the decision, not simply because it looks unpromising. Equal-valued moves can still be selected differently under different tie-breaking rules.
topics.history: Early attribution is uncertain. Knuth and Moore's 1975 account discusses McCarthy, early game programs, and independent developments. The displayed span indicates that early period; 1975 marks their analysis, not the technique's invention.

example.label: A branch that cannot win
example.code:
MAX already has an option worth 5.
A new MIN branch finds a child worth 3.
Its value can be at most 3 → prune the rest.
example.explanation: Further replies cannot make that MIN branch better than MAX's existing option.

contributors.name: John McCarthy and early game-programming teams
contributors.role: Associated with early pruning ideas; attribution and the exact form of early implementations are uncertain.

contributors.name: Donald E. Knuth & Ronald W. Moore
contributors.role: Published a detailed analysis and historical discussion in 1975.

milestones.label: Approximate early development
milestones.description: Related pruning methods emerge in several game-programming efforts; the boundaries are illustrative, not exact discovery dates.

milestones.label: Analysis
milestones.description: Knuth and Moore analyze alpha–beta and discuss its uncertain early history.

topics.title: Propositional logic
topics.tagline: Give statements a structure you can reason with.
topics.problem: An argument can sound persuasive without following from its premises. We need a language in which the structure of an inference can be inspected independently of the subject matter of its sentences.
topics.idea: Represent whole statements by symbols and combine them with connectives such as NOT, AND, OR, and implication. A truth assignment specifies a model. A knowledge base entails a conclusion when every model satisfying the premises also satisfies that conclusion. A truth table can check this directly for a small number of symbols.
topics.significance: The distinction between truth in a model and derivability by a proof procedure prepares the way for automated reasoning. Searching through assignments and searching through proofs are different computational approaches to questions expressed in logic. A connective's formal meaning need not capture every nuance of everyday language.
topics.history: Boole's 1847 book is an algebraic-logic milestone used to place this topic on the map. Propositional reasoning is much older, and the familiar modern notation and semantics developed through many contributions. The marker does not claim that Boole invented all propositional logic.

example.label: A tiny knowledge base
example.code:
P: It is raining.
Q: The ground is wet.
Premises: P, P → Q
Conclusion: Q
example.explanation: Every truth assignment satisfying both premises makes Q true.

contributors.name: George Boole
contributors.role: Developed an algebraic treatment of logic in his 1847 book.

milestones.label: Algebraic foundation
milestones.description: The Mathematical Analysis of Logic is published.

topics.title: First-order logic
topics.tagline: Talk about objects, relations, and every possible case.
topics.problem: Treating each sentence as an indivisible symbol hides its internal structure. We cannot naturally express that every student is a person, then use that general statement for a particular student, without representing objects and relations.
topics.idea: First-order logic adds variables, predicates, functions, and quantifiers over individuals. Universal quantification expresses a condition for every object in a domain; existential quantification asserts that some object satisfies it. Interpretations assign meanings to the symbols. Entailment still asks whether a conclusion holds in every model of the premises.
topics.significance: One general rule can describe many instances, making representation more expressive than a list of unrelated propositional atoms. That expressive power complicates automated reasoning: truth-table enumeration no longer provides a general decision procedure for validity over arbitrary domains. Representation and inference must be considered together.
topics.history: Frege's 1879 Begriffsschrift is a landmark in quantificational logic. His system also contains features beyond modern first-order logic. This node marks an influential foundation, not a claim that today's complete formalism appeared fully formed in one book.

example.label: From a rule to an instance
example.code:
∀x (Student(x) → Person(x))
Student(ada)
∴ Person(ada)
example.explanation: The universal statement applies to Ada without listing each student separately.

contributors.name: Gottlob Frege
contributors.role: Introduced a landmark formal treatment of quantification and inference in 1879.

milestones.label: Published foundation
milestones.description: Begriffsschrift introduces a powerful formal language for reasoning.

topics.title: Logic Theorist · early theorem proving
topics.tagline: An early program searches for proofs in symbolic logic.
topics.problem: Formal rules say which proof steps are legal, but they do not automatically tell us which step to try next. Blindly generating every possible deduction can produce an enormous search space.
topics.idea: The Logic Theory Machine represents symbolic expressions and applies proof methods while using heuristics to select promising work. Goals can be broken into subproblems; previously established results can help with later ones. A successful result is an explicit proof rather than only a yes-or-no prediction.
topics.significance: Logic supplies the language and legal transformations, while search supplies the exploration strategy. This is an early example of the relationship between the course's branches. It does not mean that this system used the later resolution algorithm, or that every modern search method descends directly from it.
topics.history: Newell and Simon described the system in 1956. J. C. Shaw contributed to its programming, documented with Newell in a 1957 implementation paper. Keeping both sources helps distinguish the authors of an individual report from the people who built the project.

example.label: A proof-search viewpoint
example.code:
Goal: establish a formula
Choose a valid proof method
Create simpler subgoals
Solve them → assemble a proof
example.explanation: This is a schematic teaching example, not a transcript of the original program.

contributors.name: Allen Newell & Herbert A. Simon
contributors.role: Developed and described the Logic Theory Machine.

contributors.name: J. C. Shaw
contributors.role: Contributed to programming; co-authored the 1957 implementation paper with Newell.

milestones.label: System description
milestones.description: Newell and Simon publish their Logic Theory Machine report.

milestones.label: Implementation paper
milestones.description: Newell and Shaw describe programming the machine.

topics.title: Resolution & unification
topics.tagline: Match expressions, then combine what follows.
topics.problem: A machine reasoning with variables must determine when differently written expressions can refer to the same case. It also needs an inference mechanism suitable for systematic proof search.
topics.idea: Unification finds substitutions that make terms agree. Resolution combines clauses containing complementary literals, using unification in the first-order case. To prove entailment, a refutation procedure adds the negation of the desired conclusion and searches for a contradiction. Translating formulas into clauses is part of this process.
topics.significance: A small inference mechanism can support a large space of possible proofs. Choosing which clauses to combine remains a search problem. Resolution's refutation completeness does not mean every unrestricted search order terminates, and it does not make arbitrary first-order validity decidable.
topics.history: Robinson's 1965 paper presents first-order resolution with unification. It does not mark the invention of all propositional resolution or every earlier term-matching idea. Prolog's restricted clause form and resolution strategy are later specializations, not simply the unrestricted procedure with a new name.

example.label: Match, then infer
example.code:
¬Student(x) ∨ Person(x)
Student(ada)
Unify x with ada → Person(ada)
example.explanation: The substitution aligns the complementary Student literals.

contributors.name: J. Alan Robinson
contributors.role: Published first-order resolution using unification in 1965.

milestones.label: Publication
milestones.description: A Machine-Oriented Logic Based on the Resolution Principle.

topics.title: Logic programming · Prolog
topics.tagline: Describe relations. Ask the system to find answers.
topics.problem: Could a program express facts and rules, then let an inference process work out how to answer a query? The challenge is to connect the meaning of a logical statement with an effective computation.
topics.idea: Prolog programs contain facts and rules; queries ask for substitutions that satisfy goals. In the usual untabled execution model, unification matches a goal with a clause, goals are explored depth-first, and backtracking tries alternatives. The core definite-clause fragment has a logical reading; practical features such as cut, side effects, and negation as failure require additional care.
topics.significance: The search branch meets the logic branch here. Rule order and goal order can change termination and efficiency even when the declarative reading looks similar. A successful query can return values for variables; a looping computation need not mean the logical claim is false.
topics.history: Colmerauer and Roussel's account describes a preliminary version in 1971 and a more definitive one in 1972, arising from natural-language work. Kowalski contributed to the logic-programming foundations and collaborated with the Marseille team. His 1974 paper is a later publication, not a cause that postdates Prolog's creation.

example.label: A first Prolog query
example.code:
parent(ada, ben).
parent(ben, cy).
grandparent(X, Z) :-
    parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

?- grandparent(ada, Who).
Who = cy.
example.explanation: Unification binds X to ada, Y to ben, and finally Who to cy. Further alternatives can be explored by backtracking.

contributors.name: Alain Colmerauer & Philippe Roussel
contributors.role: Central developers of the early Prolog project in Marseille, working with a wider team.

contributors.name: Robert Kowalski
contributors.role: Developed logic-programming foundations and collaborated with the Marseille team.

milestones.label: Preliminary version
milestones.description: An early version develops within the natural-language project.

milestones.label: Implementation milestone
milestones.description: A more definitive version of Prolog; the main marker used here.

milestones.label: Foundational publication
milestones.description: Kowalski publishes Predicate Logic as Programming Language.

topics.title: Expert systems · MYCIN
topics.tagline: Capture specialist knowledge as rules a program can use.
topics.problem: How can a program use a specialist's knowledge and explain the advice it gives?
topics.idea: An expert system separates a knowledge base from an inference engine. MYCIN used mainly backward chaining: start with a goal, then seek evidence for the rules that support it. It also handled uncertainty.
topics.significance: Expertise requires more than inference: acquiring, explaining, and maintaining rules are substantial tasks. MYCIN included consultation, explanation, and rule-acquisition components.
topics.history: MYCIN was a Stanford research system for infectious-disease consultation, implemented in Interlisp. The 1975 marker is a system publication, not the birth of all expert systems. The 1984 project account also discusses the earlier DENDRAL work in chemistry.

example.label: A schematic rule chain
example.code:
Goal: establish C
Rule: if A and B, then C
Seek evidence for A and B
Explain which rule supported C
example.explanation: A teaching sketch of goal-directed inference, not an original MYCIN rule.

contributors.name: Edward H. Shortliffe & the Stanford MYCIN team
contributors.role: Developed the consultation system and its supporting tools.

contributors.name: Bruce G. Buchanan
contributors.role: Co-edited the project's account of rule-based expert systems with Shortliffe.

milestones.label: System paper
milestones.description: The team reports explanation and rule-acquisition capabilities.

milestones.label: Project account
milestones.description: Rule-Based Expert Systems documents the MYCIN experiments.

topics.title: Building expert systems in Prolog
topics.tagline: Turn facts and rules into a small adviser.
topics.problem: Can we build an adviser without writing every step of the search ourselves?
topics.idea: Prolog's inference engine can work backward from a query through rules and facts. Merritt's book builds identification systems, then explores custom engines for explanation, uncertainty, and forward chaining.
topics.significance: A few rules make a prototype. A useful application also needs interaction, explanations, and a maintained knowledge base. Prolog's built-in search is a starting point; developers can implement other reasoning strategies.
topics.history: Dennis Merritt's 1989 Expert Systems in Prolog documents concrete construction techniques. This date anchors a published guide, not the first expert system written in Prolog.

example.label: A tiny equipment adviser
example.code:
powered(printer).
empty_paper_tray(printer).

action(Device, load_paper) :-
    powered(Device),
    empty_paper_tray(Device).

?- action(printer, What).
What = load_paper.
example.explanation: An original classroom example. The facts are supplied explicitly; this small rule base has no interactive questioning or explanation facility yet.

contributors.name: Dennis Merritt
contributors.role: Authored a practical guide to constructing expert systems in Prolog.

milestones.label: Construction guide
milestones.description: Expert Systems in Prolog presents working examples and reasoning-engine designs.

topics.title: IBM Watson · Prolog in language analysis
topics.tagline: Match language patterns with logic-programming rules.
topics.problem: A question and an answer passage may express the same relationship with different words. How can a system detect the match?
topics.idea: Watson represented parsed text as facts and used Prolog rules to detect patterns, including semantic relations and expected answer types. Unification and backtracking helped match combinations of conditions.
topics.significance: This was a specific component of the larger DeepQA system, which combined many algorithms and evidence scores. Watson was not written entirely in Prolog.
topics.history: IBM Watson won its Jeopardy! challenge in February 2011. Adam Lally and Paul Fodor's account that year explains the Prolog role in its language-processing pipeline.

example.label: From parsed facts to a relation
example.code:
subject(write1, ada).
object(write1, field_notes).
lemma(write1, write).

author_of(Person, Work) :-
    lemma(V, write),
    subject(V, Person),
    object(V, Work).
example.explanation: An original simplified illustration of pattern matching, not Watson's production rules.

contributors.name: IBM Watson / DeepQA team
contributors.role: Built the question-answering system.

contributors.name: Adam Lally & Paul Fodor
contributors.role: Described its use of Prolog in language analysis.

milestones.label: Competition and account
milestones.description: Watson wins the challenge; Lally and Fodor describe the Prolog component.

topics.title: Probability theory
topics.tagline: Describe uncertainty with consistent numerical rules.
topics.problem: An agent may not know which possible world is actual. How can it describe uncertainty without making contradictory assessments?
topics.idea: Assign probabilities to events: they are nonnegative, the whole sample space has probability one, and disjoint alternatives add. A joint distribution describes variables together; marginalization sums over alternatives. Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A,B)/P(B) requires P(B) > 0.
topics.significance: Independence is an assumption to justify, not the default: P(A,B) = P(A)P(B) only when A and B are independent. Conditional independence can hold even when marginal independence does not.
topics.history: Kolmogorov's 1933 book established an influential axiomatic foundation. Probability had a long history before it; the timeline marks this foundation rather than its invention.

example.label: One joint distribution
example.code:
wet    dry
rain         0.16   0.04
no rain      0.08   0.72

P(rain) = 0.20
P(wet) = 0.24
P(wet|rain) = 0.16/0.20 = 0.80
example.explanation: The four entries sum to one. Rain and wet ground are dependent in this original teaching model.

contributors.name: A. N. Kolmogorov
contributors.role: Published the 1933 axiomatic foundation.

milestones.label: Axiomatic foundation
milestones.description: The original German edition of Foundations of the Theory of Probability appears.

topics.title: Bayes' theorem
topics.tagline: Use evidence to revise a prior belief.
topics.problem: Knowing how likely evidence is under a hypothesis does not directly tell us how likely the hypothesis is after observing that evidence.
topics.idea: For P(E) > 0, P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E). For mutually exclusive, exhaustive hypotheses, P(E) is the sum of P(E|h)P(h). The prior matters alongside the likelihood.
topics.significance: P(E|H) and P(H|E) answer different questions. Updating can run against the direction of a model's arrows, without establishing a causal effect.
topics.history: Richard Price communicated Bayes's essay after Bayes's death; it was read in December 1763. It addressed inverse probability in a specific setting, rather than presenting the full modern Bayesian framework in today's notation.

example.label: Wet ground as evidence
example.explanation: An original example consistent with the probability card. An 80% likelihood becomes a posterior of about 66.7%, not 80%.

contributors.name: Thomas Bayes
contributors.role: Developed the inverse-probability argument in the essay.

contributors.name: Richard Price
contributors.role: Communicated the posthumous essay to the Royal Society.

milestones.label: Royal Society reading
milestones.description: Price communicates Bayes's essay; the text records a reading on 23 December.

topics.title: Bayesian networks
topics.tagline: Represent a joint distribution with local dependencies.
topics.problem: A full joint table grows exponentially with the number of variables. How can useful structure make the model more compact?
topics.idea: A directed acyclic graph gives each variable a conditional distribution given its parents. The joint is the product of those local distributions. The graph encodes conditional-independence assumptions; an edge alone does not establish causation.
topics.significance: Representation and inference are separate tasks. A compact network may still require expensive exact inference.
topics.history: Pearl's 1986 paper is a milestone in belief networks and probabilistic propagation, not a unique birth date for graphical probability models.

example.label: Extend the rain model
example.code:
Rain → Wet → Report

P(R,W,S) = P(R)P(W|R)P(S|W)
P(R=true) = .20
P(W=true|R=true/false) = .80/.10
P(S=true|W=true/false) = .90/.20
example.explanation: S is a sensor report. This original model assumes Report is conditionally independent of Rain given Wet; false-value probabilities are complements.

contributors.name: Judea Pearl
contributors.role: Developed belief-network methods and local propagation.

milestones.label: Belief-network publication
milestones.description: Fusion, propagation, and structuring in belief networks appears.

topics.title: Inference by enumeration
topics.tagline: Sum the hidden possibilities, then normalize.
topics.problem: Given a network and observed evidence, how do we calculate a distribution over a query variable?
topics.idea: Fix the evidence, evaluate each query value, and sum the joint probability over every assignment to hidden variables. Normalize the resulting weights when the evidence has positive probability. Joint entries come from the network's CPT product.
topics.significance: Enumeration is an exact baseline. It can repeat subcomputations and takes exponential time in the general case.
topics.history: Enumeration uses ordinary marginalization, with no single invention date asserted here. Its marker shares the 1986 belief-network context; Russell and Norvig provide the explicit textbook algorithm cited below.

example.label: Query Rain given a positive report
example.explanation: Wet is hidden; Report is observed. Both values of Wet contribute to each query weight.

contributors.name: Stuart Russell & Peter Norvig
contributors.role: Present the Enumeration-Ask teaching algorithm; credited as expositors, not inventors of marginalization.

milestones.label: Shared network context
milestones.description: The timeline groups this computation with the belief-network milestone, not an origin claim for enumeration.

topics.title: Variable elimination
topics.tagline: Reuse a sum instead of repeating its work.
topics.problem: Enumeration recomputes products and sums. Can the network's factorization help us avoid that repetition?
topics.idea: Restrict factors to evidence. For each hidden variable, multiply all factors containing it, sum it out, and retain the resulting factor. Multiply the remaining factors and normalize over the query.
topics.significance: The posterior is exact, as with enumeration. Elimination order controls intermediate factor sizes and can change cost dramatically; exact inference remains expensive on general networks.
topics.history: Zhang and Poole's 1994 paper documents a simple factor-based approach to Bayesian-network computation. It is one publication milestone, not a claim that all elimination ideas began with this paper.

example.label: Eliminate Wet from the same query
example.explanation: The same answer as enumeration. This tiny network illustrates the operations; larger networks expose the benefit of reusing intermediate factors.

contributors.name: Nevin Lianwen Zhang & David Poole
contributors.role: Published the 1994 factor-based computation approach.

milestones.label: Factor-based computation
milestones.description: A simple approach to Bayesian network computations appears at AI-94.

topics.title: Probabilistic logic programming
topics.tagline: Combine logical consequences with uncertain choices.
topics.problem: Logic programs describe relations, while probabilistic models describe uncertainty. Can one representation support both?
topics.idea: One influential approach assigns a distribution to basic facts, then uses logical rules to determine their consequences. The resulting possible worlds induce probabilities for queries. Probabilistic logic programming includes multiple semantics and languages.
topics.significance: It connects programming, probabilistic inference, and learning. PRISM's 1997 paper demonstrates models such as Bayesian networks and HMMs, alongside parameter learning.
topics.history: Sato's 1995 distribution-semantics paper and Sato and Kameya's 1997 PRISM paper are milestones within a broader research history. ProbLog is a later member of this family, not its starting point.

example.label: A distribution over logical worlds
example.code:
Uncertain choices → selected facts
Selected facts + rules → consequences
P(query) = total probability of worlds
           in which the query holds
example.explanation: A conceptual sketch of a distribution-semantics approach, not syntax shared by every probabilistic logic language.

contributors.name: Taisuke Sato
contributors.role: Developed the distribution-semantics framework cited here.

contributors.name: Taisuke Sato & Yoshitaka Kameya
contributors.role: Presented PRISM's symbolic-statistical modeling and learning.

milestones.label: Semantic foundation
milestones.description: Sato publishes the distribution-semantics paper.

milestones.label: PRISM
milestones.description: PRISM combines probabilistic logic programming with learning.

topics.title: Statistical relational learning
topics.tagline: Learn under uncertainty when objects are connected.
topics.problem: People, papers, and organizations have relationships. Treating each record as an isolated feature vector can discard important structure.
topics.idea: SRL brings statistical learning together with relational representations from logic and databases. Its approaches include relational graphical models and logic-based probabilistic models, with tasks such as link prediction and collective classification.
topics.significance: This is a research field encompassing several approaches, rather than one algorithm or a single language. Learning model parameters or structure differs from answering a query in a fixed model.
topics.history: The 2004 workshop preface records workshops in 2000 and 2003 and growing interest across communities. Getoor and Taskar's 2007 edited volume brought many approaches together. These are signs of a field taking shape, not a precise birth date.

example.label: A relational learning question
example.code:
Objects: papers and authors
Relations: writes(author, paper)
           cites(paper, paper)
Observed: some paper topics
Task: predict missing topics using links
example.explanation: An original task sketch. Related objects need not be independent training examples.

contributors.name: Lise Getoor & Ben Taskar
contributors.role: Edited the 2007 volume bringing together SRL approaches.

contributors.name: Tom Dietterich, Lise Getoor & Kevin Murphy
contributors.role: Co-chaired the 2004 workshop connecting SRL with other fields.

milestones.label: Workshop community
milestones.description: An SRL workshop is held at AAAI, documented retrospectively in the 2004 preface.

milestones.label: Collected introduction
milestones.description: Introduction to Statistical Relational Learning collects models, algorithms, and applications.

topics.title: Markov logic networks
topics.tagline: Weighted logical formulas become probabilistic preferences.
topics.problem: Useful generalizations can have exceptions. How can a relational model express that a rule usually holds?
topics.idea: An MLN pairs first-order formulas with weights. Over a finite domain, groundings define features of an undirected Markov network. World probabilities are proportional to exp(Σᵢ wᵢ nᵢ), where nᵢ counts satisfied groundings.
topics.significance: A weight is not a rule's conditional probability: other formulas and the normalization constant also affect the distribution. Inference and weight learning are separate tasks.
topics.history: Richardson and Domingos's 2006 journal paper combines first-order logic with probabilistic graphical models within the growing SRL landscape.

example.label: A soft relational rule
example.code:
weight w:
∀x,y  Friend(x,y) ∧ Smokes(x) ⇒ Smokes(y)
example.explanation: A schematic example: positive w favors satisfying groundings while allowing exceptions. It is not a causal assertion or a probability of w.

contributors.name: Matthew Richardson & Pedro Domingos
contributors.role: Authored the Markov Logic Networks paper.

milestones.label: Journal paper
milestones.description: Markov Logic Networks appears in Machine Learning.

topics.title: ProbLog
topics.tagline: Ask how likely a logical query is to succeed.
topics.problem: A query can have several proofs based on uncertain facts. How do we calculate its probability without counting shared cases twice?
topics.idea: In the basic independent-fact setting, each probabilistic fact is included or excluded in a sampled program. Deterministic rules derive consequences. A query's probability is the total probability of sampled programs in which it succeeds.
topics.significance: Multiple proofs may overlap, so adding their probabilities is generally wrong. ProbLog connects proof search with probability calculations over Boolean explanations.
topics.history: De Raedt, Kimmig, and Toivonen introduced ProbLog in a 2007 paper with biological-network link discovery as an application.

example.label: Two independent ways to get wet
example.code:
0.2::rain.
0.3::sprinkler.
wet :- rain.
wet :- sprinkler.
query(wet).

P(wet) = 1 - (1-.2)(1-.3) = .44
example.explanation: An original example in modern ProbLog notation. The shared case where both facts hold has probability .06; .20 + .30 would count it twice.

contributors.name: Luc De Raedt, Angelika Kimmig & Hannu Toivonen
contributors.role: Introduced ProbLog and its link-discovery application.

milestones.label: ProbLog publication
milestones.description: The IJCAI paper presents the language and query-probability solver.

connections.label: Add uncertain choices to logic programs
connections.explanation: Distribution semantics combines probabilistic facts with logical consequences; PRISM also supports parameter learning.

connections.label: Represent probabilistic models as programs
connections.explanation: PRISM's paper demonstrates Bayesian networks as symbolic-statistical programs. This connects representations, without equating every probabilistic logic language with a Bayesian network.

connections.label: A concrete probabilistic logic language
connections.explanation: ProbLog is one member of this broader family, with semantics based on query success in sampled programs.

connections.label: Attach weights to formulas
connections.explanation: Grounded first-order formulas supply features for a Markov network.

connections.label: Model uncertainty over related objects
connections.explanation: SRL includes relational extensions of graphical models and logic-based probabilistic formalisms, with both inference and learning.

connections.label: One SRL representation
connections.explanation: Markov logic is one of the logic-based approaches collected in the SRL volume.

connections.label: Overlapping research traditions
connections.explanation: The SRL volume includes stochastic logic programs and Bayesian logic programming. Probabilistic logic programming and SRL overlap, but neither names exactly the same set of work.

connections.label: Two ways to combine logic and probability
connections.explanation: MLNs use weights on formulas in a globally normalized Markov network. Basic ProbLog uses probabilities on independent choices and derives logical consequences. Their annotations have different meanings; this edge does not assert a historical lineage.

connections.label: From truth assignments to uncertainty over them
connections.explanation: A Boolean assignment specifies a possible world. Probability can put weights on such worlds when the actual world is uncertain; probabilities obey consistency rules rather than replacing the meaning of logical connectives.

connections.label: Two ways to reason from uncertain evidence
connections.explanation: MYCIN's certainty factors and a Bayesian network's probabilities are different uncertainty formalisms. Compare how each represents domain knowledge and combines evidence; this is not a claim that one system directly became the other.

connections.label: Reverse conditional probabilities
connections.explanation: Write the same joint probability as P(H)P(E|H) and P(E)P(H|E). Equating them yields Bayes' theorem when P(E) is positive.

connections.label: Factor a joint distribution
connections.explanation: The chain rule always factors a joint distribution. The network's conditional-independence assumptions let each variable depend only on its parents in the factorization.

connections.label: Update beliefs across a model
connections.explanation: Bayes' theorem relates priors, likelihoods, and posteriors. A Bayesian network represents the joint distribution from which those conditional probabilities can be computed; graph arrows do not restrict the direction of inference.

connections.label: Sum over unobserved variables
connections.explanation: Replace joint entries with products of local CPT entries, sum over hidden assignments, and normalize the query values.

connections.label: Reuse intermediate sums
connections.explanation: Both methods compute the same exact posterior. Variable elimination distributes products over sums and stores intermediate factors to avoid repeated work; ordering controls factor size.

connections.label: From logical rules to domain expertise
connections.explanation: Logical implication provides a useful classroom comparison for IF–THEN rules. MYCIN also needed uncertainty handling, domain knowledge, and a control strategy; its rules are not simply arbitrary first-order formulas.

connections.label: Implement a rule-based adviser
connections.explanation: Merritt demonstrates how Prolog can supply inference for expert-system applications and how custom engines can add capabilities. MYCIN itself was implemented in Lisp; this connection concerns a way to build systems of this kind.

connections.label: Facts and rules become an application
connections.explanation: A query can work backward from a proposed conclusion to the facts needed to support it. An interactive expert system adds ways to obtain facts, explain conclusions, and maintain its knowledge base.

connections.label: Prolog inside IBM Watson
connections.explanation: Lally and Fodor describe Watson's use of Prolog to match patterns over parsed text, including detecting answer types and semantic relations.
connections.sourceNote: Natural Language Processing With Prolog in the IBM Watson System, discussion and examples of parse facts and detection rules.

connections.label: Two frontier policies
connections.explanation: Both explore a state space. BFS uses a queue to advance in layers; DFS uses a stack to follow and then backtrack along a branch. This is a teaching comparison, not a claim of historical descent.

connections.label: From steps to weighted costs
connections.explanation: With equal positive edge weights, shortest-path cost and number of steps give the same ordering by distance. Dijkstra's algorithm handles unequal nonnegative weights by prioritizing accumulated cost.

connections.label: Add an estimate of what remains
connections.explanation: A* adds h(n) to accumulated cost g(n). Setting h = 0 recovers uniform-cost ordering; on a finite nonnegative-weight graph, this matches Dijkstra-style shortest-path expansion up to stopping rules and tie-breaking.

connections.label: Traverse a game tree depth-first
connections.explanation: A recursive minimax implementation can traverse the game tree depth-first and back up values. DFS determines an exploration order; minimax determines what those values mean.

connections.label: Apply adversarial evaluation to chess
connections.explanation: Shannon's chess formulation evaluates possible replies using minimax-style reasoning. Its depth-limited scores approximate positions that are not terminal game outcomes.

connections.label: Prune without changing the value
connections.explanation: Alpha–beta skips branches that cannot affect the minimax value on the same fixed search tree. It is an optimization of the search, not a different objective.

connections.label: Two meanings of a heuristic
connections.explanation: A* estimates a remaining path cost; a chess evaluator estimates a position's desirability. Both use domain knowledge, but their quantities and guarantees differ. This connection is pedagogical.

connections.label: Add objects, relations, and quantifiers
connections.explanation: The course moves from whole-statement atoms to predicates about individuals. This describes a relationship between modern formalisms, not a claim that Frege simply extended Boole's system.

connections.label: Search for symbolic proofs
connections.explanation: The Logic Theory Machine operates on symbolic logic expressions and seeks proofs. Logic defines the task; heuristic search helps choose the work to attempt.

connections.label: Proofs also have choice points
connections.explanation: A maze and a proof problem can both be understood as searches among alternatives. This teaching analogy does not assert that Trémaux directly influenced the Logic Theorist team.

connections.label: Automate clause-based inference
connections.explanation: Robinson's method reasons with first-order clauses, using unification to align literals. A proof procedure operates on a representation; the two are distinct ideas.

connections.label: A documented theorem-proving lineage
connections.explanation: Colmerauer and Roussel describe the team's work with Robinson's resolution principle and their 1971 encounter with Kowalski and SL-resolution. This documents an influence on the project, without treating all resolution strategies as identical.
connections.sourceNote: The Birth of Prolog, historical sections 2.1–2.2 (PDF pp. 3–7).

connections.label: Search by backtracking
connections.explanation: Traditional untabled Prolog execution explores alternatives depth-first with backtracking. This is a use of a search strategy, not evidence of a direct personal influence from the nineteenth-century maze work.

connections.label: Give rules a procedural reading
connections.explanation: The definite-clause core connects a logical reading of rules with goal-directed computation. Prolog is not a complete terminating reasoner for arbitrary first-order logic.
